metadata.file_name: 32. Resinoet al. (2024). Student well-being and mathematical literacy performance in PISA 2018  a machine-learning approach.pdf
metadata.title: Student well-being and mathematical literacy performance in PISA 2018: a machine-learning approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (secondary analysis of the OECD database) and models mathematical literacy using ten plausible values, selecting plausible value 8 for the tree-based models. The authors report preprocessing steps (multiple imputation by chained equations for missing values, centering/scaling of continuous predictors, and removal checks for near-zero variance) and then fit models that account for the nested student–school structure via hierarchical linear models (random-intercept at school level). However, the manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any PISA weight variables (e.g., student-level design weights). Because the analysis combines ML algorithms (decision tree, random forest) with multilevel regression, the weighting strategy should be clarified for population-representative inference; without explicit weight use, results may reflect an unweighted analytic sample.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Spanish student body that participated in PISA 2018 (ages 15–16). The analytic sample is described as the full Spanish PISA 2018 participant set (35,943 students), with preprocessing that includes multiple imputation for missing values and subsequent random split into training (70%) and validation sets for the ML models. No additional grade/school-type restriction is reported beyond the PISA 2018 target population; school-type composition is described (state, state-funded, private).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (Spain, ages 15–16; mathematical literacy; plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Decision Tree (regression tree): selected PV8 with RMSE = 82.985 (max depth = 3; min obs/node = 25; min obs/terminal = 100). Random Forest: selected PV8 with RMSE = 75.579 (401 trees; max depth = 25; 10 variables).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for Spain, the study leveraged well-being questionnaire domains—especially social well-being indicators such as communication with parents’ partners and time with friends—along with physical and material well-being variables to predict mathematical literacy, finding that social well-being variables were the most influential and that Random Forest achieved lower prediction error than regression trees (RMSE 75.579 vs 82.985). This indicates that strengthening students’ supportive social relationships (with teachers, peers, and family contexts) may be a practical lever for improving mathematics outcomes, though the study’s cross-sectional design and PV-based modeling limit causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (Spain; multilevel random-intercept models with PV-based outcome)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematical literacy performance (multilevel regression; Model 2 with 15 well-being predictors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel models: Model 1 (with ESCS controls) explained 61.004% of variance; Model 2 (adds 15 well-being variables) increased explained variance to 66.912% and reduced deviance from 204589.486 to 202344.578 (X² = 2668.188; gl = 17; p = .000). ICC decreased from 12.675% (Model 1) to 5.656% (Model 2). Significant coefficients included: ESCS +23.101; average ESCS +25.122; talk to mother’s partner −16.102; talk to teacher +20.757; friends days after school −20.494; physical education class days (0 or 3+ days) −31.573.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for Spain, the study leveraged socioeconomic context controls (student and school ESCS) and the top well-being predictors from the ML step within multilevel random-intercept models to explain mathematical literacy, finding that adding student well-being variables increased explained variance from 61.004% to 66.912% and reduced between-school variance (ICC from 12.675% to 5.656%). This indicates that well-being—particularly social well-being and supportive communication with teachers—may meaningfully co-vary with mathematics performance beyond socioeconomic status, suggesting that school climate and relational supports could be prioritized in interventions, while causality cannot be inferred from non-experimental data.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 for Spain (N=35,943; ages 15–16) to examine how student well-being questionnaire variables relate to mathematical literacy. The dependent variable is mathematical literacy based on ten plausible values; the authors select plausible value 8 for the ML models and then estimate multilevel random-intercept regression models (student level 1, school level 2) to quantify effects while monitoring ESCS. For prediction, Random Forest outperforms regression trees, achieving lower RMSE on the selected plausible value (75.579 vs 82.985) and identifying social well-being variables (communication with parents’ partners and time with friends) as the most important predictors. In the multilevel models, adding 15 well-being predictors increases explained variance from 61.004% to 66.912% and reduces ICC to 5.656%. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal claims) and incomplete reporting of survey-weight usage for population-representative inference.
